_comment: The committed seccomp syscall allowlist of the sandboxes.
app_spec.xml, Untrusted Code Sandbox, feature 160:
System applies a seccomp syscall allowlist, which rejects a process
attempting a disallowed syscall
(docs/nullius-tech-architecture.md section 5.2: the control table's own
row is 'Syscalls | seccomp allowlist', and section 3's zone map states
the posture that row serves - 'Z1 - Mutated by the loop | Signal code,
exploration policy code | LLM agents | Sandboxed: no network, no FS,
seccomp, cgroup limits'; section 15's failure table gives a violation
its consequence - 'Sandbox escape attempt | seccomp violation | Kill,
record fail_class, quarantine the node and its subtree' - and the Kill
in that row is what default_action below is written from).
The compile in packages/sandbox/src/sandbox/syscalls.py refuses this
file and any change to it that is not a well-formed allowlist with a
denying default action, so the ceiling below is not a convention the
next edit can forget: it is the configuration, checked, and a process
attempting a syscall it does not name is rejected with the code
disallowed_syscall.
Why the two keys, and why 'default_action' is one of them. A seccomp
filter is an allowlist only if everything not listed meets a *denying*
action - a filter whose default is SCMP_ACT_ALLOW admits every syscall
the list does not mention, which is not a narrower box but no box at
all. So the file states the action rather than leaving it to a
launcher's default, and the compiler refuses 'allow' (and the other
non-denying actions: log, trace, notify) by name. The two actions that
do reject are both legal and they are different facts: 'kill' is
section 15's row - the process dies on SIGSYS - while 'errno' hands the
process back EPERM and lets it keep running. This deployment commits
'kill', because section 15's recovery column is where the violation's
consequence is written down, and a box that returned EPERM instead
would be a box whose process kept executing after an escape attempt.
What the ceiling covers, and why each cluster earns its place:
- read, write, readv, writev, close, lseek, fcntl, dup - the payload
channel's own calls. Section 5.2 gives the box no mounts and no
network, so the only descriptors it holds are the IPC channel's
(feature 159's payload-only rule, feature 166's Arrow IPC); these are
how the window arrives and how the score vector leaves;
- pipe2, poll, ppoll, epoll_create1, epoll_ctl, epoll_wait, eventfd2 -
the event plane the channel's readiness is waited on with. Present
and not merely tolerated: a box that could not wait on its channel
would busy-loop, and a busy-loop is a cpu budget spent on nothing
(feature 162's cpu.max);
- brk, mmap, munmap, mprotect, madvise, mremap, membarrier, rseq - the
heap. The payload is a materialized window over the whole universe
and polars and pyarrow allocate into it, so a filter that refused
mmap would refuse every signal that can legally run; membarrier and
rseq are in for a determinism reason rather than a memory one -
glibc registers them at startup and their absence changes a
library's synchronisation path silently, which is the class of
invisible difference feature 164 exists to prevent;
- rt_sigaction, rt_sigprocmask, rt_sigreturn, sigaltstack - the
interpreter's own signal handling, which CPython installs whether or
not a signal uses it. Note what is NOT here: kill, tgkill and tkill,
because a box that could signal a process could signal one outside
itself;
- futex, sched_yield, getpid, gettid, set_tid_address,
set_robust_list, arch_prctl, prlimit64, uname - the runtime's own
bookkeeping. prlimit64 is worth its own sentence: CPython and glibc
read their own RLIMIT_* at startup, and the fact that the box can
read an address-space limit is NOT the cgroup limit feature 162
measures - the two are different mechanisms with different failure
modes, exactly as budget_policy.json's own comment argues for its
two memory numbers. futex is present because the interpreter's GIL
is built on it and feature 164 has already pinned the numerics to one
thread; the pin is the law about threads and this is the law about
syscalls, so neither duplicates the other;
- clock_gettime, nanosleep - the monotonic clock CPython, the allocator
and the channel's waits read for their own internal deadlines. The
wall-clock reads a signal could turn into a feature are policed at
the search seam by feature 139's call-level floor, which composes
with this ceiling rather than being duplicated by it - the same
division imports_allowlist.json states for datetime and random;
- exit, exit_group - the process's own termination. The compiler
requires at least one of these to be present, because a filter that
admitted nothing would kill the box at its first instruction and the
deployment would never learn what it refused: 'we admitted nothing'
and 'we safely refused everything' are different facts, and only the
second is a control. That is deliberately the opposite reading from
imports_allowlist.json's, where an empty ceiling is legal - a screen
that admits nothing refuses a module *before* it runs and returns
that refusal as a value the pipeline records, while a syscall filter
that admits nothing leaves nobody to do the recording.
Absent by design, cluster by cluster, because each absence is the
posture section 5.2 states in its control table:
- open, openat, openat2, creat, stat, fstat, lstat, newfstatat, statx,
readlink, readlinkat, getdents64 - every filesystem read. Section
5.2's row is 'No mounts. Data arrives over IPC only.', so there is
nothing to open; the modules the box may import are named by feature
167's ceiling and are loaded into the interpreter image the box runs
on, and the window arrives over the channel (feature 166) rather
than from a file;
- socket, socketpair, connect, bind, listen, accept, accept4, sendto,
recvfrom, sendmsg, recvmsg, setsockopt, getsockopt - every network
call. Feature 158 denies egress at the namespace layer ('a namespace
with no interfaces. Not a firewall rule.'); this is the second
mechanism, and a deployment that believes it needs one of these has
a bug in the first;
- ptrace, process_vm_readv, process_vm_writev, pidfd_open, kcmp - the
escape surface proper, and the syscalls a seccomp bypass is usually
written with. Section 15's failure table is about these;
- ioctl - the one file-descriptor operation a box does not need and
the one whose danger is argument-dependent. A seccomp filter cannot
express 'TIOCSTI is refused and the rest are fine' without
argument-level matching, and a filter that admits ioctl wholesale
admits the classic terminal-injection primitive; the channel's own
reads and writes do not need it;
- clone, clone3, fork, vfork, execve, execveat - the box is one
process pinned to one thread (section 5.2's env clause, feature 164).
A signal that forks is contained at the cgroup layer by feature
162's pids.max and refused at this layer by the filter; the two are
the same posture enforced at two distances, which is why both are in
section 5.2's table and why neither is a substitute for the other;
- getrandom - deliberately absent, and this is the one absence a reader
is most likely to read as an oversight. Section 12's determinism row
passes the seed into signal() and stores it on the node (feature
165), and section 5.2's own call site sets PYTHONHASHSEED=0 in the
box's env; a box that could draw kernel entropy could produce a
vector no replay reproduces, which is the P3 failure feature 165's
suite exists to prevent. The absence of this syscall is what makes
that environment variable mean something;
- unshare, setns, mount, umount2, pivot_root, chroot, capset,
personality, seccomp - the namespace, mount and filter-manipulation
surface. A box that could install a wider filter over itself would
be a box whose ceiling is advisory.
This is one allowlist for every box the isolation policy covers - the
feature's own sentence says 'a seccomp syscall allowlist', singular,
and the two Z1 boxes of isolation_policy.json run under the same
ceiling this file is.
